extracted.intended_audience: bacteriology students and laboratory technicians preparing culture media
extracted.subtask_description: Step-by-step laboratory procedures and standards for preparing, standardising, filtering, tubing, sterilising, and storing nutrient media (bouillon, gelatine, agar, blood-serum, etc.) for bacteriological work. Includes recipes, physical/chemical controls, and handling/storage guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food requirements for bacteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure parasites will not live outside the living body; facultative parasites need highly organised foods (proteids, nitrogen/carbon sources, salts); saprophytic bacteria require non-concentrated food and are more easily cultivated; some bacteria will grow in almost pure distilled water or in pure carbohydrate solutions; water is absolutely essential to growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use media approximating the natural pabulum of the organism. Choose richer proteid-containing media for facultative parasitic bacteria and simpler carbohydrate or watery media for saprophytes. Ensure media are not overly concentrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reaction of media (pH) for bacterial growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth is most active in media which react slightly acid to phenolphthalein — that is, neutral or faintly alkaline to litmus. Mould growth is most vigorous in media strongly acid to phenolphthalein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine and adjust media reaction; different organisms have specific optimum reactions. Use phenolphthalein as indicator for accurate assessment (see titration protocol).

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric requirements (oxygen classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisms requiring oxygen are 'obligate aerobes'; those that thrive equally with or without oxygen are 'facultative anaerobes'; those requiring exclusion of free oxygen are 'obligate anaerobes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide appropriate oxygen conditions when cultivating: aeration for aerobes, reduced or no oxygen for obligate anaerobes, and flexible conditions for facultative types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature ranges and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Few bacteria grow below 5°C or above 40°C; 30–37°C is most favorable for most micro-organisms. Bacteria classified by optimum temperature: psychrophilic (min 0, opt 15, max 30 °C), mesophilic (min 15, opt 37, max 45 °C), thermophilic (min 45, opt 55, max 70 °C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select incubation temperatures according to organism class. Know the thermal death-point (temperature causing death of vegetative forms after 10 minutes) for sterilisation planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light exposure effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Many organisms indifferent to light; light frequently impedes growth and alters biochemical characters (chromogenicity, liquefaction). Pathogenic bacteria undergo progressive loss of virulence when cultivated in presence of light. Some water-derived organisms are photogenic (phosphorescent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control light exposure as part of environmental conditions; cultivate light-sensitive organisms in darkness or reduced light to preserve virulence and expected properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movement/agitation effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Slight movements (flowing) do not injure growth; violent agitation (shaking) absolutely kills bacteria. A condition of perfect rest is most conducive to bacterial growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vigorous agitation during incubation unless protocol requires it; ensure stability for optimal growth of most organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of metabolic products (identification criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacteria produce pigments (chromoparous/chromophorous/parachromophorous), enzymes (proteolytic, diastatic, invertin, rennet), toxins (extracellular and intracellular), and metabolic end-products (organic acids, alkalies, aromatic compounds, reducing substances, gases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe pigment, enzyme, toxin, and metabolic end-product production as diagnostic criteria; consider environmental factors (oxygen, light, temperature) that influence these outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of solidifying agent and liquefiable vs solid media
rubrics_metrics.description: Many media are fluid but rendered solid by adding gelatine or agar. Gelatine media in commonly used percentages become fluid at ~25°C; agar-solidified media liquefy at ~90°C and solidify at ~40°C. Some media (potato, coagulated blood-serum) cannot be re-liquefied and are 'solid' media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose gelatine when incubation at room/cold temperatures is intended (gelatine melts at ~25°C). Choose agar when media must remain solid at higher temperatures or be re-liquefied by heat. Be aware of reagent behavior on cooling/heating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration specifications for solidifying agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Example proportions given: 10 per cent. gelatine, 2 per cent. agar. The designation refers to quantity of substance added during manufacture, not percentage present in the finished medium (commercial products contain insoluble material removed by filtration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the stated concentrations when preparing media; account for insoluble material in commercial agar/gelatine when calculating final composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness and sterility of apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Scrupulous cleanliness is to be observed with regard to all apparatus, vessels, funnels, etc., employed in preparation of media; although in preliminary stages absolute sterility is not essential for most media preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain high cleanliness standards; sterilise at appropriate steps (see sterilisation regime). Avoid contamination especially during filtration, tubing, and storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meat extract preparation proportions and method
rubrics_metrics.description: Meat extract: extract half a kilo meat with 1 L water for ordinary strength, or 1 kg meat with 1 L water for 'Double Strength' extract. Heat gently not exceeding 40°C for first 20 minutes, then boil for 10 minutes, strain and filter, make up to volume, sterilise in steam steriliser for 20 minutes on each of three consecutive days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer heart muscle (bullock's/sheep's heart) for best extract. Alternative: use commercial meat juices (Brand's, Wyeth's, Lemco) but may be unsatisfactory for highly parasitic bacteria. Follow temperature/timing strictly for stable extract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardisation of meat extract reaction before titration
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolonged boiling causes hydrolytic changes increasing acidity; meat extract becomes stable after being maintained at boiling-point for 45 minutes. Accurate estimation of reaction requires (1) exposure to 100°C for 45 minutes, (2) estimation performed at boiling-point, and (3) phenolphthalein as the indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always boil samples 45 minutes before titration and run titration at boiling temperature with phenolphthalein to obtain reproducible titre values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titration method and expression of titre
rubrics_metrics.description: Titrate 25 c.c. of medium at boiling point against standard NaOH solutions using phenolphthalein; express titre as number of cubic centimetres of normal alkali per litre required to render solution neutral to phenolphthalein. Prefix '+' if original solution reacts acid, '-' if alkaline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform control titrations for accuracy. Use properly standardised NaOH solutions (10N, n/1, n/10). Report titres like 'meat extract +10' meaning 10 c.c. normal NaOH per litre needed for neutrality to phenolphthalein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target standard reaction for routine nutrient media (+10)
rubrics_metrics.description: For most bacteria the 'optimum' reaction approximates +10; this is adopted as the standard for nutrient media derived from meat extract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardise media to +10 by subtracting 10 from initial titre to find amount of alkali to add per litre. Use decinormal solutions where bulk changes must be minimal. Example calculations provided in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtration techniques and filter folding
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluid media usually filtered through stout Swedish filter paper folded as the 'physiological filter' (detailed folding steps provided). Liquefiable solid media filtered through papier Chardin (ready-folded). Filters should be moistened with hot distilled water before use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fold Swedish filters in the physiological shape to maximize surface area and speed filtration. Use appropriate filter type for gels (papier Chardin). Maintain funnels and filters warm when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hot-water funnel and heating for agar filtration
rubrics_metrics.description: If agar is badly 'egged' or during cold months, surround the glass funnel with a hot-water jacket (water at about 90°C) supported on a ring gas burner; alternatively, place flask and funnel inside a steam steriliser and filter in an atmosphere of live steam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep agar warm during filtration to prevent premature solidification and slow filtration. Use hot-water funnel or steam chamber as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sterilisation regime (discontinuous method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sterilise media in the steam steriliser at 100°C for 20 minutes on each of three consecutive days (discontinuous method). Specific durations vary: nutrient bouillon and gelatine 20 minutes; nutrient agar 30 minutes for each of three days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the discontinuous sterilisation schedule to stock media. Note different media may require altered times (e.g., agar: 30 min x 3). Ensure flasks/tubes are properly plugged during sterilisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tubing and volumetric filling of media
rubrics_metrics.description: After filtration, media usually 'tubed' — filled into sterile tubes in definite measured quantities, usually 10 c.c. Use separator funnel with a three-way tap and calibrated receiving cylinder (e.g., Treskow's funnel or improvised apparatus). Carbohydrate-containing media filled into fermentation tubes or tubes with inverted small tubes to collect gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reliable three-way tap arrangements; calibrate receiving cylinder carefully. For gas-forming bacteria use Durham tubes; ensure small tubes are submerged after final sterilisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storing bulk media and sealing
rubrics_metrics.description: After filtration fill medium into sterile litre flasks with cotton-wool plugs, sterilise 20 minutes x 3 days, then cut off top of plug, push plug down and fill neck with melted paraffin wax to mouth level. Preferably use long-necked flint glass bottles with special rubber caps that seal after sterilisation. Store in cool dark cupboard or iron safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sealing with paraffin or specially designed rubber caps helps maintain sterility and prevent evaporation. Store media in cool, dark, as airtight as possible a cupboard or safe labelled 'media stores'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storing tubed media (packing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pack tubed media vertically in oblong boxes (internal 37 cm x 12 cm x 10 cm) with movable partition (weighted triangular block or sliding flat piece) and celluloid label for medium name. Arrange boxes on shelves in dark cupboard or iron safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pack vertically to avoid spillage and make identification easy. Label boxes and maintain dark, cool storage to preserve media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of egg whites (albumen) for clarification of gelatine/agar
rubrics_metrics.description: After cooling medium to 60°C, well whip whites of two eggs, add to flask, steam at 100°C until albumen coagulates and forms large firm masses floating in clear gelatine/agar, then filter through papier Chardin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Egg albumen coagulation precipitates impurities aiding clarification before filtration. Perform at specified temperatures/times for effective clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipes and ingredient proportions for common stock media
rubrics_metrics.description: Example recipes: Nutrient bouillon — double strength meat extract 500 c.c., distilled water 300 c.c., Witte's peptone 10 g (1%), salt 5 g (0.5%); Nutrient gelatine — double strength meat extract 500 c.c., peptone 10 g, salt 5 g, 100 g sheet gelatine; Nutrient agar — double strength meat extract 500 c.c., peptone 10 g, salt 5 g, 20 g powdered agar; specific heating, filtration, titration and sterilisation steps follow each recipe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow weighing/taring and volumetric steps precisely. Use double strength extracts to allow for dilution during steam processing. Follow the complete sequence: dissolve, titrate, adjust reaction, steam, filter, tube, sterilise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and weighing procedures (accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh flasks on trip balance or counterpoise, calculate water required to make up to 1 litre by difference, add boiling distilled water from wash-bottle until pans balance. Use pipettes graduated to hundredths and burettes in tenths for titration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise weighing and volumetric techniques to ensure correct concentrations and final volumes. Employ counterpoises and calibrated apparatus for accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling carbohydrate-containing and gas-forming media
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluid media with carbohydrates are filled into fermentation tubes or tubes with inverted small tubes to collect gas (Durham tubes). When first filled small gas tubes float after first sterilisation but after final sterilisation they should be submerged and filled with the medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate tube types for gas detection; ensure correct filling and placement so gas production is captured and observable after final sterilisation.
